videos.title: Siegfried Müller Fails to Save The Congo - The 2nd Battle of Boende, 1964
videos.desc:
On September 17th Siegfried Müller launched Operation Tshuapa. With no map, no radio, and equipment of dubious reliability, he aimed to drive 320 kilometres into barely charted jungle and save the Congo with only a few dozen men. It went about as well as could be expected.

This is part two in a four part series covering 'Operation Tshuapa', the two month battle over a town very few had ever heard of that held the fate of the Congo. And a battle that briefly made 52 Commando and SIegfried Muller infamous celebrities.

videos.title: When Belgium, The Congo, and the CIA fought Cannibals in the Jungle - The 1st Battle of Boende, 1964
videos.desc:
The battles for Boende, from September to October 1964, could be argued as the point at which the Simba rebellion failed. What started as a continuation of their lightning offensive across the North of the Congo that began when Stanleyville fell in August of that year, ended up being their high-water mark. It could have however, for a very tense few weeks, gone either way, especially considering some of the major defeats that were inflicted on the Congolese, some of which were accomplished without even firing a shot.

videos.title: Siegfried Muller - From German Artilleryman to Congo Mercenary
videos.desc: Of all the mercenaries from the early days of the cold war, few have had the impact of Siegfried Muller. Unlike the Commanders like Mike Hoare or Bob Denard who led multiple large scale operations, or the ideologues like Jean Schramme or Rafal Gan-Ganowicz, Muller only spent roughly six months as a mercenary. Despite this the fact that the media took an instant interest in the German soldier with the iron cross combined with his willingness to self promote in interviews meant that his screen presence far outweighed his real impact.
